product.title: Levantine Arabic 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero in Levantine Arabic — the everyday dialect of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. All Arabic text is fully vowelled, with a pronunciation guide under each line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Levantine builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of the letters with their Levantine sounds, a guide to the differences between Damascus, Beirut and Amman, an A1 grammar summary, and a table of the most frequent verbs. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the ق that isn't pronounced to بدي, which isn't a verb.

blocks.text: There's one disappointment that almost everyone who has studied Arabic knows. You've put in years — at school, at university, or reading the Qur'an — you can read without vowel marks, you know hundreds of words. Then you land in Amman, open your mouth in a café, and don't understand a single sentence of the reply.

That isn't your fault, and it doesn't mean your studies were wasted. What's happening is simple: the Arabic taught in classrooms is **Fusha** (Modern Standard Arabic), the language of writing and the news, while the language people actually live in is **dialect**. Both are Arabic, both are legitimate, but they're used in different places — a bit like the English of a formal speech compared with how you talk at a market stall. The difference is that in Arabic the gap between the two is much wider.

This book teaches the second, and one particular kind of it: **Levantine Arabic** — *šāmi*, اَلشَّامِي — the dialect spoken in Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. Around forty million speakers, one stretch of land where everyone understands everyone else without the slightest difficulty.

Why Levantine, out of so many dialects? Three reasons, all of them practical. **First, it's the dialect other Arabs understand most easily**, because Syrian and Lebanese dramas have been watched from Morocco to Oman for the past thirty years. **Second, it's the closest to Fusha** of the major dialects — much closer than Moroccan, and a little closer than Egyptian — so whatever Arabic you already have gets put to real use. **Third, it's the one you're most likely to need**: work, study, travel through Jordan, humanitarian work, or simply understanding what people say on the news.

blocks.title: What should be clear from page one
items: **This book doesn't replace Fusha or compete with it.** Fusha remains the language you use to read, write letters and follow sermons and speeches. Levantine is the language you use to *talk to people*. Ideally you have both, in whichever order you like.

**Levantine has a written form but no official spelling.** People write it on WhatsApp, in song lyrics, in film subtitles — with the same Arabic letters. This book uses the most common spelling, the one closest to the Fusha form, so the words you learn can still be found in a dictionary.

blocks.text: There's a big gift waiting for you inside, and you should know about it now to keep your spirits up: **Levantine Arabic is much simpler than Fusha.** There are no case endings — word endings don't change with their role in the sentence. There's no compulsory dual (*muthanna*). Verbs have fewer forms. And in many ways the sentence structure is closer to English than Fusha's is.

And there's one big trap you should accept in unit 1, not unit 10: **in Damascus, Beirut and Amman the letter ق is not pronounced *q*.** It becomes a hamza — a catch in the throat. قَهْوَة isn't *qahwa* but *’ahwe*. It feels wrong for three days, then it becomes normal. The next pages settle it once and for all.

The twenty units cover the whole framework of Levantine Arabic at A1: greetings and introductions, where you're from and what you do, family, numbers and prices, bargaining, ordering coffee and food, telling the time, daily routines, asking the way, talking about yesterday, making plans, seeing a doctor, and the etiquette of visiting — which in the Arab world isn't an extra but the heart of the matter.

Each unit is one sitting: twenty to thirty minutes. The dialogues are short and deliberately sound like real conversation, not a textbook. Under each line you get the pronunciation, then a natural English translation, then a **word-for-word** translation — the Arabic word order forced into English. The last one often sounds strange, and that's exactly the point.
An opening phrase you'll hear a lot: يَلَّا، مِنْبَلِّشْ! *(yalla, mnballesh — come on, let's begin!)*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This book works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This book follows the Assimil approach: you don't memorize a list of rules and then try to build sentences; you absorb whole sentences first and let the rules follow. That's why the order in which you work through each unit matters.
Six steps for each unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, out loud, without looking at the meaning.** All the Arabic in this book is fully vowelled, so there's no word whose sound you have to guess. Sound first, meaning later.

**Read it again, looking at the lines underneath.** The second line (small green letters) is the pronunciation, the third is natural English, and the fourth (in italics) is the **word-for-word** translation following Levantine word order.

**Read the notes.** That's where the real content of the book lives. The notes explain why a sentence is the way it is, and almost always point to one typical learner's mistake — often a mistake that comes precisely from knowing Fusha.
**Read the grammar boxes**, then go back to the dialogue and find the examples. A rule you've just read sticks much better when you find the evidence in the sentences yourself.
**Do the exercises on paper, not in your head.** The answer key is at the end of the unit — cover it first.

**The next day, reread the previous unit's dialogue** before starting a new one. Five minutes. This is what separates people who finish twenty units and remember them from those who finish and forget.

blocks.text: Three tips specific to dialect

items: **Don't argue with the dialect.** You'll often find forms that are "wrong" by the Fusha rules you know: dropped endings, swapped letters, new words that aren't in a Fusha dictionary. That's not the speakers' mistake; that's simply the language. Accept it as it is, the way you accept "gonna" in spoken English.
**Imitate, don't analyze.** Dialect is mastered by ear. If you can get hold of Fairuz songs, Syrian TV series or Jordan's Roya news channel, one hour of listening is worth three hours of reading.
**Use a little, but every day.** Ten sentences that come out spontaneously are worth more than a hundred filed neatly in a notebook.

front.title: Pronunciation guide: two marks you must tell apart

blocks.text: The pronunciation in this book follows the conventions of the English edition of our Fusha course: plain letters for familiar sounds, a dot underneath for the "heavy" consonants. There are just two marks you really need to learn, and they look alike but sound completely different.

Letter
How it sounds
Example
Meaning
rows: from deep in the throat, a squeezed sound with no English equivalent
hamza — a catch in the throat, like the break in "uh-oh"

blocks.title: How to remember the two marks
items: **‘** opens to the right like a wide-open mouth — that's ع, and it takes effort in the throat.
**’** closes to the left like a door being shut — that's hamza, and it means a sound that is *stopped*.
Swapping them is no small slip: **سَاعَة** *saa‘a* (hour) and **سَاقَة**… isn't a word. But **عَمّ** *‘amm* (uncle) and **أَمّ** *’amm* (mother — the Fusha form) really are a dangerous pair.

blocks.text: The rest of the letters

Notice that **ح** and **ه** are both written *h*. You can tell them apart from the Arabic script: ح is heavy and breathy, like breathing on a glass to clean it; ه is light, like English *h*. The dotted letters ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ are the "heavy" versions of s d t z; kh is the *ch* of Scottish *loch*, and gh is a gargled r.
Vowels: two new ones

head: Written

rows: short; e is always pronounced, as in "bed"
**long e**, like "they" without the y at the end
**long o**, like "go" without the w at the end

blocks.text: These last two vowels are the clearest sign that what you're hearing is Levantine. In Fusha, بَيْت is read *bait* and يَوْم is read *yaum* — two sounds each. In the Levant they merge into one long sound: *bēt*, *yōm*. Once your ear picks up this pattern, hundreds of words open up. And a final **-e** is never silent: *madrase* is three syllables, mad-ra-se.

blocks.title: Word stress isn't marked — and doesn't need to be
items: Levantine Arabic almost always puts the stress on the long syllable closest to the end. Since long vowels are already marked in the pronunciation (aa, ii, uu, ē, ō), the stress falls into place if you read them as written.
If all the syllables are short, the stress goes on the first one: **كَتَبِتْ** *kátabet* (I wrote).

blocks.title: Three letters that shift — and why you mustn't panic
items: **The letter ق becomes hamza.** This is the most striking change and the most important. It applies in the cities: Damascus, Beirut, Amman. In rural Jordan and southern Palestine, ق is pronounced **g** instead (as in *gaal* for قَال). In Fusha and in Qur'an recitation it stays **q** — and nobody will be confused.

**The letters ث and ذ soften into t and d.** The form تْلَاتِة *tlaate* (three) comes from ثَلَاثَة · and هَاد *haad* (this) from هٰذَا. In the villages they stay th and dh. This book uses the city forms, because that's what you'll hear most.
**Everything else is the same.** The letters that give non-Arabs the most trouble — ع ح خ غ ص ض ط — don't change at all. If you can already pronounce them, everything you've learned still counts.

blocks.text: One more typically Levantine feature you'll meet straight away: a word-final **ة** is often pronounced **-e**, not **-a**. مَدْرَسِة is read *madrase*, not *madrasa*. This is called *imāla*, and it's a hallmark of the Damascus–Beirut accent. In Jordan and Palestine it more often stays *-a*. Both are correct; this book uses **-e** because it's the form you'll hear most in films and songs.

Arabic has lent thousands of words to Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Swahili, Malay and Indonesian — and a few hundred to English, from *algebra* and *coffee* to *sugar* and *magazine*. What's interesting: **many of them are part of everyday life in the Levant, not just religious texts.** If you know any of these languages, here are words you can use right away.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Eight words whose meaning has shifted — careful
items: The word **مَبْسُوط** *mabsuuṭ* means **happy, pleased**. Not "spread out", as in Fusha. It's one of the most frequent words in the whole Levant.
The word **دَقِيقَة** *da’ii’a* means **minute**, not "precise".
The word **مُشْكِلِة** *mushkile* means an ordinary everyday **problem**, not something especially "difficult" or complicated.
The word **جَرِيدِة** *jariide* means **newspaper** — and nothing else.
The word **مَصَارِي** *maṣaari* means **money**. It has no Fusha equivalent, and it's a word you'll use every day.
The word **شُغْل** *shughl* means **work, job**. You'll hear it constantly, from "how's work?" to "I'm busy".
The word **حَكِي** *haki* means **talk, speaking**. It has nothing to do with "hakim" (judge).
The word **غَدَا** *ghada* means **lunch**, while "tomorrow" is **بُكْرَا** *bukra*. Don't mix them up.

blocks.text: And three words you'll hear dozens of times a day in the Levant, with no one-word equivalent in English: **يَعْنِي** *ya‘ni* ("I mean…", a filler that works like "like" or "so"), **مَعْلِيش** *ma‘lēsh* ("never mind", said to comfort someone or as a light apology), and **خَلَص** *khalaṣ* ("done", "enough", "finished", "oh well" — depending on the tone).

blocks.title: Four rules that decide the verb form
items: **Present and habits take b-** · بِشْرَب ’ahwe kill yōm (I drink coffee every day).
**In progress takes عَم in front of b-** · عَم بِشْرَب ’ahwe halla’ (I'm drinking coffee right now).
**Future takes رَح, and the b- DISAPPEARS** · رَح إِشْرَب ’ahwe (I'll drink coffee).
**After بَدِّي، لَازِم، مُمْكِن، فِيني, the b- DISAPPEARS too** · بَدِّي إِشْرَب ’ahwe (I want to drink coffee).

back.title: Damascus, Beirut, Amman, Jerusalem: the differences worth knowing

blocks.text: These four cities speak one language, and their speakers understand each other without the slightest difficulty. What differs is a small set of words and sound habits — roughly the distance between London and Manchester English. Here are the ones you'll meet most.

blocks.title: What this book uses, and why
items: This book uses the **Damascus–Beirut** forms, because they're what you hear most in films, TV series and songs — and therefore what Arabs outside the Levant recognize best.
If you're heading to Jordan, change three things. The word هَلَّق becomes هَسَّا · the ending **-e** becomes **-a** (madrase becomes madrasa) · and be ready to hear ق pronounced **g** outside Amman.
If you're heading to Palestine, add one more: **مْنِيح** is often replaced by **كْوَيِّس** *kwayyis*, a word also used in Egypt.

blocks.text: One thing that often surprises learners: **the Lebanese mix in French, while Jordanians and Palestinians mix in English.** *Bonjour* and *merci* in Beirut are as ordinary as *hi* and *thank you* in Amman. It's not a sign they can't speak their own language — it's simply how people talk there, and you're welcome to join in.

If you've reached this page after working seriously through all twenty units, you can already do something most people who study Arabic for years can't: **start a conversation with an Arab and keep it going.**
What you can already do

items: Greet people, introduce yourself and make small talk properly — including the small talk that's required and the kind that's just a nicety.
Ask and answer questions about origin, work, family, where you live and daily routines.
Shop, bargain, order food and coffee, and pay without falling back on English.
Tell the time, make appointments and plan for tomorrow.
Talk about yesterday — the full past tense for all eight persons.
Say what you want, must, may and can do; turn things down politely; apologize and comfort.
Ask the way and understand the answer, including the commands رُوح and لِف.
Visit people and host them with the right etiquette.

blocks.text: Three ways to keep going

items: **Move up to Levantine A2.** Waiting for you there: the derived verb forms (فَعَّل، تْفَاعَل، اِنْفَعَل) that make your vocabulary grow in families, conditional sentences with إِذَا and لَو, tighter connectors, and longer stories with a clear time order.

**Add Fusha as its partner.** Now is actually the best time: the sentence framework is already in your head, so all you need to add is case endings and written vocabulary. The **العربية 101** course in the Linguo catalog is designed for exactly that.
**Soak your ears.** One hour a day of Syrian films or Fairuz songs beats three hours of memorizing. Start with Arabic subtitles, not English ones.

blocks.title: One last piece of advice
items: Levantine speakers are among the most patient people anywhere with foreigners who try their language — and they'll praise you lavishly after three words. Accept the praise with **يِسْلَمُوا** *yislamu*, and keep talking. Stopping out of embarrassment is the only way to fail.

If you forget a word mid-sentence, don't go silent. Say **شُو اِسْمَا…؟** *shu isma…?* ("what's it called…?") — Arabs say it every day, and the person you're talking to will almost always guess the word for you.

blocks.text: The most fitting farewell for the last page: اللَّه مَعَك. *(alla ma‘ak — God be with you.)* See you in the next book.
